## The tip

> Where the question came from, and what the reader will do with the answer.

## Frame

> Decision the reader should be able to make · headline claim (state it before building) · counter-narrative to rule out · audience and their prior knowledge.

## What the data can and can't say

> Can say / can't say (but readers might assume) / could say with more ingest. Name unresolved tensions so they travel forward explicitly.

## Hypotheses & falsifiers

> Set before looking, each with a named falsifier (H1, H2…). Close the loop with a 'what survived the reporting' audit.

## Sources & provenance

> What fed this. Point at references/ and sources/_provenance.jsonl; for datasets name the generator, inputs, cut date, and rebuild command.

## Priors ledger

> Each shift: claim · prior → posterior · shift size · confidence · source.

## Decisions

> Resolved forks and why (D1, D2…). The why is the payload — the what is recoverable from git, the why isn't.

## What's not in the piece

> Honest omissions — what you left out, and why.

## Workflow notes

## Gaps & self-critique

> Where this work is weakest; what a hostile reviewer would attack first.

work.title: What we can actually say about hydration and rise time
work.body:
# What we can actually say

Higher hydration shortens rise time [C1] — now verified: the
community trial [F1] and our own twelve bakes [F2] agree, and the
two are independent measurements, not echoes of each other. The
trial alone couldn't carry it (flip refused, correctly); the
kitchen log is what earned the verification.

Scope honestly: one flour lot, one kitchen, home-oven conditions.
Whether the effect size transfers to rye is the question we chose
not to chase [D1] — white flour only, this round.
